Literature review The interaction and interconnectedness of bank development and stock market devel- opment have been of serious research interest over the last several decades. The earli- est discourses on bank and stock market interactions (financial development) focused on growth hypotheses: financial repression, technical innovation, and supply-leading or demand-following hypotheses (see Schumpeter (1934), McKinnon (1973) and Shaw (1973) King and Levine (1993a, b, c)). Other studies, such as those of Galbis (1977), Fry (1978), Goldsmith (1969), Greenwood and Jovanovic (1990), Thakor (1996), and Hicks (1969), have viewed financial development from the perspective of the interaction of banks and the stock market as a vital driver of economic growth. Later studies have advanced the discussion in the direction of complementarity, coevolution, and substitut- ability of the market-based and bank-based measures of financial development (see, for example, Demirguc-Kunt and Maksimovic, 1998, and Levine and Zervos 1998 and, more recently, Arize et al. 2018). The debates and arguments on stock market and bank interactions have followed linear assumptions with little or no consideration of the likelihood of a nonlinear and asymmetric interface. Following Arize et al. (2019), nonlinearities and asymmetric reac- tions in bank and stock market relations can be motivated by the following: (i) Heterogeneous (individual and institutional) investors and managers who have dif- ferent investment strategies, (ii) market participants could have different expectations and beliefs about rising market capitalization compared with declining market capitali- zation and may not adjust their investing patterns by the same proportion, (iii) banks could be subject to different pressures depending on the state of the business cycle; there is a greater aversion to economic downturns and the general decline in earnings than to expansions; and finally, there could be different types of banks’ reactions following small, large, negative and positive market capitalization variations. For example, where inves- tors and market participants overreact to bad news and underact with good news, the adjustment to equilibrium may be nonlinear. Several authors have proposed likely triggers for asymmetry and nonlinearity in stock market and bank integration dynamics. These factors include the presence of informa- tion barriers, asymmetries, and other sources of market segmentation (Bekaert and Harvey (1995)), heterogeneous transaction costs Anderson (1997), the coexistence of different shareholders, and noise trading De Grauwe and Grimaldi (2006). Global monetary policy uncertainty (GMPU) and bank development The relationship between bank sector development (BD) and global monetary policy uncertainty (GMPU) is theoretically ambiguous. GMPU has a risk aversion effect and an expected future profit‒risk effect. The negative impact stems from the fundamental option theory, which arises from the risk aversion effect. This theory holds that bank sector developments can be lessened with increased GMPU (see, among others, Ber- nanke and Reinhart. 2004; Dixit 1983), postulates that uncertainty creates an incentive for firms to delay investment when the option to delay is available. Furthermore, the the- ory predicts that uncertainty can have consequences when there is a degree of irrevers- ibility—the higher the degree of uncertainty is, the more firms benefit from postponing investment projects. Given that GMPU creates ambiguity among economic agents, it can induce them to invest less or more depending on their degree of risk tolerance. This is common with banks, which may try to avoid bank risk by reducing their investment/ financial services in the current period. On the other hand, the ‘risk-loving’ behavior of economic agents might lead to the expected future profit‒risk effect, positively impacting bank development. When uncer- tainty reaches a point where losses are enormous, a risk-averse bank may increase its investment/financial services by reorganizing production or raising the supply of invest- ment activities to compensate for the drastic loss in revenue or avoid any decline in its future revenue. Faced with an increasingly high degree of risk aversion with decreasing income, a firm will increase activity to prevent the risk of cash flow and income effects, thereby causing activities to share a positive relationship with uncertainty and risk. For banks, as the option value for waiting increases with a higher level of uncertainty, the likelihood of making a better, more informed decision increases until uncertainty dimin- ishes. In summary, while the real option argument can reduce the level of economic out- comes such as investment and consumption, it also causes economic agents to be less sensitive to changes in business conditions, hence tending to make bank development rise side by side with increasing levels of uncertainty (see Drobetz et al. (2018)). Works by García-Kuhnert et al. (2015), Pathan (2009), and Uhde (2016) argue that a fall in output could lead to lower economic activities and an increased need for financial services, which reduces the income diversification capacity of commercial banks. This A rize et al. Financial Innovation (2026) 12:2 Page 7 of 30 leads to the expected profitability effect as the earnings of commercial banks decline significantly. Additionally, bank managers might have profit motives, causing them to engage in risk-taking behaviors with excessive credit supply to obtain higher potential returns. Moreover, a weakened economy would limit possible credit supply projects for banks. As a result, bank managers often feel pressured by profitability targets and may be motivated to take more risks in their credit activities. In addition, diversified wealth portfolios of agents could lead to less risk aversion. Banks whose controlling sharehold- ers are more diversified and, therefore, less risk averse are more willing to undertake risks and riskier projects and are less concerned about banks’ day-to-day risk operations. However, real options models ignore competitive interactions among agents. Grenadier (2002) shows that competition could erode the value of the option to wait. These find- ings imply that EPU may positively affect bank development depending on the dominant side of credit, be it demand or supply. Theories that are predicated on the banks’ incentive to search for yield and agency relationships in bank ownership and management have been found to incentivize risk- taking. Firms make less investment and employ less labor in periods of increased uncer- tainty, which would result in lower demand for credit and, consequently, a narrowed interest margin for banks. However, the return target required by shareholders may not change immediately with the decline in banks’ profit, thus inducing banks to allocate their assets toward “high-risk-high return” projects. Earnings transparency theory can also influence uncertainty, bank development, and interaction. Policy uncertainty has important economic consequences because the con- tent and timing of policy changes can increase uncertainty regarding profitability and current and future adverse events. An examination of the relationship between uncer- tainty in economic policy and bank earnings opacity can establish this. We hypothesize that policy uncertainty is positively associated with earnings opacity, as the opportu- nities to distort earnings are greater during periods of high policy uncertainty since it increases the information asymmetry between management and external stakeholders, thus making it more difficult for investors and creditors to assess the existence and mag- nitude of hidden “adverse news.” If investors and creditors cannot observe the under- lying economic conditions, managers are more likely to withhold “adverse news” that would otherwise negatively affect their self-interest. Conclusions and policy implications This paper was inspired by the need to determine the elasticity of bank and stock market development in the context of monetary policy uncertainty. As bank and stock market development are known to adapt to shocks arising from the uncertain business envi- ronment, investigating the degree and direction of such adaptation is both a policy and research necessity. What sets this investigation apart is the use of a combination of linear and nonlinear models, a departure from previous studies, which we believe will pique your interest. The geography of this study is the Nigerian economy, one of Africa’s largest economies. The authors believe that using Nigerian data contributes to a better understanding of the financial market forces in an emerging economy whose characteristics differ from those of developed economies. It is also an exposition of some key economic relationships that have hitherto been ignored. The key takeaways from the study include the following: • That bank development in Nigeria responds asymmetrically to global monetary pol- icy uncertainty. • Thus, reducing uncertainty has a more substantial positive effect than increasing uncertainty does. It will undoubtedly reshape the empirical understanding of the relationship between bank development and stock market development. This study challenges the assumption of linearity of the linkage and considers the impact of uncer- tainty in the economic climate, providing a broader perspective. This study challenges the assumption of linearity in the linkage and considers the impact of uncertainty in the financial environment, thereby broadening the narrative and enlightening the reader. Three significant conclusions anchored on our findings are of policy interest. First, based on the empirical evidence from this study, positive and negative economic cli- mates drive bank development. The banking industry is highly regulated, so the bank’s regulatory environment and operational mechanisms can be adapted to suit the chang- ing business environment. Against the backdrop of changing business climates, this strengthens banks’ adaptability. Moreover, this makes banks adaptable to optimistic and adverse business climates, a finding that engages the reader in the discussion. On the other hand, LUP has a negative long-term linear relationship with market development, whereas the positive partial sum of LUP contributes to the weakening of stock market development. A possible explanation is that the stock market is more sensitive to policy uncertainty than to bank development; that is, the stock market is more exposed to global financialisation than the banking sector is. This thought is also shared by Huang et al. (2023), who observed that there is much uncertainty in the global financial system due to trade, political, and unforeseen issues and that these uncertain- ties distort the stability of the financial system. On the other hand, expansionary and contractionary monetary policies have increasing effects on the stock market and bank development. This stresses Nigeria’s financial system’s adjustment capacity to deliberate policy changes and the unintended consequences of economic policy uncertainty. The right-sided error correction and the bound test results all confirm the long-run elasticity of the stock market and the banking sector with respect to monetary policy and uncer- tainty dynamics. In a country such as Nigeria, with an overwhelming dependence on oil and no clear policy roadmap for revenue-source decoupling, the resource curse, capital flights, and the rippling effect of economic monolithism may continue to create uncer- tainties and limit the growth of the financial system (see Uche and Effiom 2021; Yacouba Altıntaş and Bilgili, 2020 and Yacouba and Altıntaş 2020). This will be the case if no proper policy or regulatory safety nets are put in place. Second, the results show that the capacity variable, industrial production, did not sig- nificantly impact bank or stock market development. This finding proves that produc- tivity is driven primarily by the financial system, which provides the financial resources needed to lubricate the production ecosystem. This strengthens the argument of the supply-driven hypothesis of the finance growth nexus. Notably, including the capacity variable and the imposition of asymmetric variables improved our model formulation. Thus, on the basis of the exclusion test results, the correct formulation of the bank devel- opment model for Nigeria should include market capitalization, industrial production, monetary measures, and economic uncertainty as determinants. The omission of eco- nomic uncertainty in prior studies tends to overstate the elasticity estimates of the mon- etary variables in absolute terms. This has been addressed in the current study. Third, the study uncovered evidence in support of asymmetry and nonlinearity in the relation- ship between bank development and stock market development with an established long-run relationship (cointegrating vectors) and error-correction term coefficients that are between 0 and 1, indicating that the relationships have no oscillatory explosion and hence can be predicted. The knowledge of the shock transmission pattern (asymmetric/ nonlinear) and the predictability of this relationship will guide policymakers and indus- try players in controlling and exploring the system. This, undoubtedly, would be a way to channel financial resources from the stock market and banks to the overall benefit of the economic system and the economy. In terms of relevance to the Nigerian economy and similar economies, the NARDL results can yield several policy recommendations. First, policymakers should focus on building safety nets against global monetary con- ditions, as a drop in uncertainty has a highly positive impact on bank development. However, a sudden sharp drop in uncertainty may lead to over lending and financial bubbles requiring prudential regulations. Such practical policies can effectively stabilize banking activities during unusual times and events while maintaining economic stability and mitigating potential risks. Additionally, prudent monetary policy measures are recommended to mitigate tur- moil in lending markets by enhancing the sentiment of investors and customers. Recapi- talization in the Nigerian banking industry has been ongoing, and efficient banks (those with lower costs per income and profitability) are encouraged to improve their capital base by reinvesting their profits and approaching the stock market for capitalization. Sufficiently capitalized banks become rightly positioned to meet regulatory require- ments and engage in profitable operations while maintaining the confidence of the bank- ing public. This is necessary for the Nigerian financial system, which is bank dominated. It is further recommended that policies send credible and high-quality credit signals to reduce credit constraints for corporate participants, households, and market par- ticipants (corporate or household sectors). Such strong efforts are likely to reduce non- performing loans, as they are indicators of systemic risks and financial crises. This will essentially contain uncertainties and will continually stabilize the financial or economic system. A rize et al. JSON: Name: bank_stock_nonlinear_nardl_nigeria Title: Nonlinear ARDL (NARDL) estimation of asymmetric effects of global monetary policy uncertainty on bank and stock market development in Nigeria Short Hypothesis: Changes in global monetary policy uncertainty cause asymmetric effects on Nigeria's bank development (credit-to-GDP) and stock market capitalization-to-GDP such that positive and negative shocks of equal magnitude produce statistically different long-run elasticities. Related Work: Prior empirical work on the bank–stock market nexus predominantly employs linear cointegration and VAR/ARDL frameworks and often reports complementarity, substitutability, or coevolution between banks and markets. Limitations of existing approaches include reliance on annual data, symmetric linear specifications that cannot detect sign-dependent responses, insufficient treatment of structural breaks and hidden cointegration, and omission of high-frequency global monetary uncertainty measures. Some studies use nonlinear techniques (threshold, Markov-switching) but do not jointly test short-run and long-run asymmetries across all regressors or quantify dynamic multipliers. Few analyses exploit partial-sum decompositions to separate positive/negative shocks or apply bound-testing methods adapted for asymmetric cointegration, and robustness to seasonality, small-sample bias, and alternative uncertainty indices remains underexplored. Abstract: This research operationalizes a structured empirical pipeline to quantify asymmetric causal effects of global monetary policy uncertainty on bank development and stock market capitalization in Nigeria. The approach combines high-frequency monthly macrofinancial series with a global monetary policy uncertainty index and applies linear ARDL and nonlinear ARDL (NARDL) models based on partial-sum decomposition to estimate short-run and long-run asymmetric elasticities and dynamic multipliers. The pipeline includes unit-root testing with structural-break detection, optimal lag selection, bounds testing for cointegration, Wald tests for long- and short-run asymmetry, and a suite of residual and stability diagnostics. The main contribution is a reproducible experimental design that identifies whether positive versus negative uncertainty shocks produce statistically distinct responses in credit-to-GDP and market-cap-to-GDP, and measures the speed of adjustment to equilibrium. Expected outcomes are precise long-run elasticity estimates, short-run reaction profiles, evidence on hidden cointegration, and documented robustness across alternative specifications and samples. Experiments: Datasets: monthly 1990M01–2022M04 from Central Bank of Nigeria (credit to private sector, broad money M2, stock market capitalization, industrial production), IMF IFS where needed, and Global Monetary Policy Uncertainty (GMPU) index (monthly). Preprocessing: transform series to logs and scale by GDP where applicable; construct positive and negative partial-sum series for each regressor. Baselines: (1) OLS in levels (for benchmarking), (2) linear ARDL bounds-testing model, (3) VAR/VEC as alternative dynamic baseline, (4) threshold-ECM. Proposed model: NARDL with partial-sum decomposition of GMPU, M2, MCAP, CPS, and IP. Unit-root and structural-break tests: ADF/Perron-type tests with endogenous break detection. Lag selection: Schwarz (BIC) with maximum lag = 8 for monthly data. Estimation steps: (a) estimate linear ARDL(p,q,...) and perform bounds F-test for cointegration; (b) estimate NARDL with decomposed regressors and compute long-run coefficients; (c) Wald tests for long-run (β+ = β−) and short-run symmetry; (d) compute dynamic multipliers and cumulative responses for horizons up to 24 months. Evaluation metrics: F-bounds p-value, t-statistics for long-run coefficients, ECM coefficient magnitude and significance, AIC/BIC, adjusted R2, residual diagnostics (LM for autocorrelation, ARCH test, White heteroskedasticity, RESET), stability tests (CUSUM, CUSUMSQ), out-of-sample 1–12 month RMSE, Diebold–Mariano test comparing predictive accuracy of NARDL vs ARDL. Robustness and ablation: (i) omit GMPU to measure omitted-variable bias, (ii) include crisis dummy and sample splits (pre-2008 vs post-2008), (iii) use alternative uncertainty indices (global EPU vs GMPU), (iv) bootstrap standard errors (2,000 replications) for small-sample inference. Additional analysis: Monte Carlo power analysis to evaluate size/type-I error of asymmetry Wald tests under sample length and noise levels. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement error and construct validity in the GMPU index may bias coefficient estimates; GMPU may imperfectly capture the relevant monetary-policy channel for Nigeria. Endogeneity and reverse causality between financial development and uncertainty can invalidate causal interpretation if not adequately addressed. Structural breaks, regime shifts, or unmodeled I(2) behavior would violate NARDL assumptions and produce spurious inferences. Small-sample and monthly-frequency issues may reduce power and produce size distortions for asymmetry tests. Model sensitivity to lag selection, partial-sum windowing, and inclusion/exclusion of control variables can produce unstable coefficient estimates. Seasonal patterns, data revisions, or missing observations in historical series may contaminate results. Results derived for Nigeria may not generalize to other countries with different financial structures or to periods with extreme global shocks not represented in the sample. Computationally, extensive bootstrap and Monte Carlo robustness checks increase runtime but not model validity in the presence of fundamental misspecification.
